What's the use case for +P rounds? I can see there's more mass to the bullet. Is there a larger powder charge as well?

Not sure why you asked this here ... but I don't mind answering :)

+P means the pressure is higher than 'standard'. If you put a more powerful charge in the casing, it'll shoot the bullet faster in general, but the pressure will be higher.

Sometimes people feel the +P is harder to make quick shots with because it recoils more. For me it depends on the load.

The pressure also has to do with how much space there is. If there is a long bullet that weighs less (like 115gr Corbon DPX) it will need to set back further and the pressure will be higher. Corbon DPX is a good bullet because it is solid copper, but because copper weighs less than lead, you can't push the 115gr DPX as fast as you could a traditional lead bullet (because the copper bullet is longer).

I'll use +P usually in my Glock 43 9mm but depending on the load the recoil can be a lot greater.

Well hopefully that makes sense :)

Oh and some manufacturers don't recommend +P it depends If you have a Glock it is no problem.
Is this for greater penetration, or does higher FPS result in a flatter trajectory?

Faster will make it flatter, but with handguns I think usually people are thinking to use them within 30 yards or so. The .357 sig is often noted for shooting nice and flat because it goes faster than a 9mm.

I'd say +P is more energy. A +P round can push the same weight bullet faster. Often this is for greater penetration, yes. But it depends on the bullet. A hollowpoint that is designed to expand might penetrate less if it is faster because the extra velocity makes it open up faster and expel energy quicker actually.

All in all I'd probably prefer +P if I found I could control the round, but not with every bullet. Depends on the bullet design. This Gold dot is pushed beyond its design threshold and falls apart.
